concept.title: Inheritance and default values
concept.shortdesc: The cascade selects a cascaded value for a property on an element. CSS then determines the property’s specified value. If no declaration supplies a cascaded value, inheritance or the property’s initial value provides the default.

section.title: Inheritance
section.p: CSS Cascade 5 §7.2, Inheritance.
Some properties inherit automatically. Their definitions say whether they are inherited. A child element uses the parent’s computed value unless a declaration gives the child another value.
section.pre: chapter { color: navy; } title { color: teal; }
section.p: The title uses teal. Other descendants inherit navy. A property that does not normally inherit uses its initial value when it has no cascaded value.
Inheritance follows the XML element tree. It is not determined by whether the property describes text, a box, or another feature.

section.title: CSS-wide keywords
section.p: CSS Cascade 5 §7.3, Explicit Defaulting.
CSS-wide keywords can be used as the complete value of any property. They affect defaulting after the cascade has selected the declaration.
CSS Cascade 5 §7.3.1, Resetting a Property: the initial keyword.
initial selects the property’s initial value from its definition. It does not mean the value inherited from the parent, even for a property that normally inherits.
CSS Cascade 5 §7.3.2, Explicit Inheritance: the inherit keyword.
inherit uses the parent’s computed value, whether or not the property normally inherits. At the root, where there is no parent, it uses the initial value.
CSS Cascade 5 §7.3.3, Erasing All Declarations: the unset keyword.
unset acts like inherit for a property that normally inherits. It acts like initial for a property that does not normally inherit.
section.pre: chapter { color: unset; } title { margin-left: unset; }
section.p: The first declaration follows the normal inheritance behavior of color. The second uses the initial value of margin-left.
CSS Cascade 5 §7.3.4, Rolling Back Cascade Origins: the revert keyword.

revert removes declarations from the winning declaration’s origin for that property and runs the cascade again. For an author declaration, this means the author-origin value is rolled back so a lower origin can supply a value. If no declaration remains, normal defaulting and inheritance apply.
section.pre: title { color: navy; } title { color: revert; }
section.p: CSS Cascade 5 §7.3.5, Rolling Back Cascade Layers: the revert-layer keyword.

revert-layer removes declarations from the winning declaration’s layer at that origin and reruns the cascade. A declaration in a lower-priority layer can then win. If no declaration remains in that origin, the cascade can fall back to a lower origin.
The theme declaration rolls back to the base layer’s value.

section.title: The all property
section.p: CSS Cascade 5 §3.2, Resetting All Properties: the all property.
The all property accepts a CSS-wide keyword and applies it to nearly every property. It does not affect direction, unicode-bidi, or custom properties.

This uses each property’s normal unset behavior. Inherited properties inherit; other properties use their initial values. Use all carefully because it can reset declarations from many unrelated property groups.

section.title: A declaration invalid after the cascade
section.p: CSS Variables 1 §2.3, Resolving Dependency Cycles; CSS Variables 1 §3.1, Invalid Variables.

A value can pass the declaration’s initial syntax check and become invalid later, for example when a var() reference has no usable value or substitution produces text that does not match the property’s grammar. The cascade has already selected that declaration. CSS does not return to an earlier, lower-priority declaration for that property; the invalid-at-computed-value-time declaration acts as unset.
This differs from a declaration that is invalid before it enters the cascade. An invalid declaration is discarded, so another valid declaration can win.
